The Renaissance. A transformative cultural and artistic movement spanning roughly the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, beginning in Italy and radiating across Europe. Rooted in the rediscovery of classical Greco-Roman texts and values, the Renaissance reoriented art, literature, and thought toward humanism, naturalism, and the celebration of individual genius.

In visual art, the Renaissance marked a shift from the flat, symbolic registers of medieval work to illusionistic representation, anatomical accuracy, and perspective—a revolution that defined Western art for centuries. The Renaissance began in Italy, especially Florence and Rome, in the fourteenth century, where wealthy merchants and patrons like the Medici family sponsored artistic innovation. Classical revival was central: artists and scholars looked to ancient Rome and Greece as models for beauty, proportion, and human achievement.

Humanism placed emphasis on individual worth, intellectual inquiry, and the study of ancient texts, reshaping both art and philosophy. Technological advances—particularly improved oil painting, the printing press, and developments in optical theory—enabled new artistic possibilities. The Italian Renaissance produced Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael, whose works became paradigmatic for Western art. Perspective, anatomy, and observational naturalism replaced the symbolic, flattened forms of medieval art.

The Northern Renaissance, in Flanders, Germany, and beyond, developed parallel but distinct innovations, including oil painting and an emphasis on portraiture. The Renaissance gradually gave way to Mannerism and the Baroque as artistic priorities shifted in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
